On the ann-benchmarks GloVe-100 dataset, the fastest methods answer 60 to 850 times more queries per second than a full scan, depending on the recall target. Recall against exact search is only part of the story: after reranking, retrievers with far lower recall reach almost the quality of exact search (see Key Takeaway 6).

Vectors come from learned embeddings or from perceptual features such as color histograms. They are compared either with a similarity score, where larger is better (dot product, cosine), or with a distance, where smaller is better (Euclidean, Manhattan). The comparison function belongs to the feature. Length normalization turns cosine similarity into a plain dot product, and on the unit sphere ranking by Euclidean distance equals ranking by cosine.

Classical spatial indexes (Voronoi diagram, grid file, R-tree) were built for two and three dimensions. The optimal algorithm of Hjaltason and Samet runs on all of them and needs only an optimistic bound per region, so it also works for the dot product. Even in 2D, a nearest-neighbor search follows several paths, because it must prove that no closer point exists.
The curse of dimensionality is quantifiable. Distances grow like

children.value: while their spread stays constant, so the contrast between the nearest and the farthest point vanishes, and dot products of random vectors concentrate around zero. Once the expected nearest-neighbor distance exceeds the size of a leaf, even the optimal algorithm visits every leaf, and decades of R-tree variants did not change this.

Loss of contrast also weakens the meaning of “nearest”. Real data still works because related items form clusters that stand out from the background, but within a cluster the exact nearest neighbor is just one of several good matches. Vector search often serves as a first stage whose candidates a reranker reorders, and even without a reranker users want good matches rather than the single best one. Both arguments justify trading exactness for speed.

Approximate search pulls three levers. Fewer dimensions (PCA, Matryoshka) is a modest lever that still reads every vector. Fewer bits per vector (scalar quantization, product quantization, LSH) makes every comparison cheaper; the compression errors are small compared to the gap between good matches and the background, and the VA-file shows that bounds on the quantized cells even keep the search exact. Fewer vectors read (IVF, HNSW) visits only the regions near the query. Combined, the levers cut the work per query by two to three orders of magnitude, but their errors compound, so their parameters must be tuned together, on end-to-end quality rather than on recall alone.

Recall against exact search understates the quality of approximate search. On TREC-COVID, retrievers that read hundreds of times less data than a full scan return only a quarter of the exact top 10, yet after reranking many come within a few points of exact search, because the documents they return instead are often just as relevant. A reranker repairs fine-filter errors, such as coarse PQ codes, but not coarse-filter errors, such as unprobed IVF lists, so the coarse filter should stay generous.

In practice, vector search lives inside libraries (FAISS, Lucene), search engines (OpenSearch), and databases (pgvector). Realistic queries combine a vector search for meaning, a keyword search for names and terms, and filters for hard constraints. Filters are applied before, after, or during the search: pre-filtering suits selective filters, post-filtering suits graph indexes that deliver a stream of candidates, and filtering during the search suits the list scans of an inverted file.
